en.title: Calendar and dates
en.goal: Talk about days of the week, full dates and times, and set up a meeting.

lessons.dias-semana: Saying the days of the week
lessons.hora-encontro: Saying the exact time and setting up a meeting

phrases.t: What day of the week is it today?
After 10 o'clock I'm not at home.

dialogue.title: Setting up a meeting
lines: What day of the week is it today?
Then let's meet on Sunday, okay?
Great! After 3 p.m. I'm free all the time.

weekdays.title: How the days of the week are built
weekdays.body: The days of the week in Chinese follow a very logical pattern: 星期 (xīngqī, "week") followed by a number from 1 to 6 for Monday to Saturday. Sunday is the exception, using 星期天 or 星期日 instead of a number.

dates.title: How full dates are built
dates.body: A full date in Chinese goes from largest to smallest: Year + 年 + Month + 月 + Day + 号 — unlike English dates, which put the month or the day first.

hao-vs-ri.title: "Hào" is what you SAY — "rì" is what you WRITE
hao-vs-ri.body: Hào (号) is the form you'll hear in everyday speech for the day of the month. In formal texts, documents and written dates, it's common to see rì (日) instead — the same character that appears in 星期日 (Sunday).

hours-minutes.title: Hours with minutes
hours-minutes.body: To say a time with minutes, just put Number + 点 (hour) + Number + 分 (minute) in a row — very direct, with no extra words between them.

yiqian-vs-yihou.title: "Yǐqián" or "yǐhòu"?
yiqian-vs-yihou.body: Yǐqián (以前) means "before". Yǐhòu (以后) means "after". Both always come after the time or event they refer to — in English, "before" and "after" come first ("before 10").
examples: after 10 o'clock I'm not at home
